title: Given a singly linked list L0 to L1 to ... to Ln, reorder it to L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln-1 to L2 to Ln-2 and so on. You may not change node values, only rearrange the nodes themselves.
shortTitle: Reorder List (L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln-1) — Find Middle, Reverse, Merge

s1_definition.profdef: Reordering a list into the L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1 pattern is a three-phase in-place technique: find the middle with fast and slow pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves by alternating one node from the front half and one from the reversed back half. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank has a queue of customers numbered 1 to n and wants to reseat them so the first and last sit together, then the second and second-last, and so on, to pair high-priority with low-priority for fair processing. A clerk finds the middle of the queue, turns the back half around so it faces front, then zips the two halves together one person at a time, front, back, front, back.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split at the middle, reverse the back half, then interleave front and back node by node.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reordering a list into the L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1 pattern is a three-phase in-place technique: find the middle with fast and slow pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves by alternating one node from the front half and one from the reversed back half. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank has a queue of customers numbered 1 to n and wants to reseat them so the first and last sit together, then the second and second-last, and so on, to pair high-priority with low-priority for fair processing. A clerk finds the middle of the queue, turns the back half around so it faces front, then zips the two halves together one person at a time, front, back, front, back.

**One line to remember:** Split at the middle, reverse the back half, then interleave front and back node by node.

sections.s2_technical:
The reorder pattern interleaves the list with itself from both ends. Doing it with O(1) space requires three well-known subroutines combined.

Phase one finds the middle. We use fast and slow pointers: `ListNode slow = head, fast = head; while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }`. After this, slow is the end of the first half. We then split by taking `ListNode second = slow.next; slow.next = null;` so the first half is cleanly terminated.

Phase two reverses the second half with the three-pointer reversal: `ListNode prev = null, curr = second; while (curr != null) { ListNode next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next; } second = prev;`.

Phase three merges by alternating. We take one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, repeatedly: `while (second != null) { ListNode f = first.next; ListNode s = second.next; first.next = second; second.next = f; first = f; second = s; }`. The careful part is saving the next pointers before we overwrite them so we do not lose the rest of either list.

A senior-level nuance is splitting the list evenly. For an even length, both halves are equal; for odd length, the first half gets the extra node, so the merge terminates correctly when the second half runs out. Getting the fast-pointer loop condition right, using fast.next and fast.next.next, ensures the first half is never shorter than the second, which keeps the interleave clean.

Another nuance is that this problem forbids changing values, so we must physically relink nodes, which is why pointer bookkeeping matters more here than in value-swap approaches.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes a daily queue of loan applications in arrival order, but the risk team wants them reordered so each pass pairs the earliest application with the latest, then the second earliest with the second latest, to balance review workload between fresh and aged cases. This exact interleave-from-both-ends pattern is the reorder list problem.

Problem 2 — The queue is stored as a singly linked list and can be large, so we reorder in place without extra memory, using middle-finding, reversal, and alternating merge.

Problem 3 — We must not alter the application identifiers, only their order, so the algorithm relinks nodes rather than copying or swapping field values.

In the code: a `LoanNode` holds an application id, a BigDecimal amount, and a next pointer. A `QueueReorderService` has a `reorder` method with the three phases. A `ReorderDemo` main builds a six-application queue and logs the reordered sequence.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6.

Step 1: Fast and slow find the middle. After the loop, slow is on L3. We set second to L4 and cut L3.next to null. First half is L1, L2, L3. Second half is L4, L5, L6.

Step 2: Reverse the second half. L4, L5, L6 becomes L6, L5, L4, with second pointing at L6.

Step 3: Merge by alternating. Take L1, then L6, then L2, then L5, then L3, then L4. We carefully save each next pointer before overwriting. When second runs out after placing L4, the merge stops.

Final order: L1, L6, L2, L5, L3, L4.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reordering a linked list into the L zero, L n, L one, L n-minus-one pattern is a classic three-phase in-place algorithm that combines three well-known subroutines. First I find the middle using the fast and slow pointer pair and split the list into a front half and a back half. Second I reverse the back half using the three-pointer reversal. Third I merge the two halves by alternating one node from the front with one node from the reversed back, carefully saving each node's next pointer before I overwrite it so I never lose the remainder of either half.

The whole thing runs in linear time and constant extra space, and because the problem forbids changing node values, every step physically relinks nodes rather than copying field values, which is why the pointer bookkeeping in the merge phase is the part I pay the most attention to.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, the risk team processes a daily queue of loan applications and wants them reordered so each pass pairs the earliest application with the latest, then the second earliest with the second latest, which balances review workload between fresh and aged cases. The queue is a singly linked list, and this reorder algorithm produces exactly that front-and-back interleaving in place.

The subtle correctness point I always mention is how the list splits. By using the fast-dot-next and fast-dot-next-dot-next loop condition, the front half is never shorter than the back half, so on both even and odd lengths the alternating merge terminates cleanly when the back half runs out, with the leftover middle node on odd lengths correctly ending up last.
